title: Everyday Verbs
summary: All five verb types in the present, minulla on, the genitive and the partitive, for shopping and café visits.

lessons.title: Five verb types
lessons.objective: Recognise the five verb types from the infinitive and use the present-tense endings.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Every Finnish verb belongs to one of **five verb types**. You can see the type from the end of the **infinitive**, the dictionary form. The type tells you how to find the **stem**. Then the present-tense endings are the same for every type: `-n, -t, (long vowel), -mme, -tte, -vat/-vät`.

cards.title: Remember type 1
cards.body: Recap from World 1, type 1: remove the last `-a/-ä` and you have the stem: `puhu|a` → `puhu|n`. The `hän` form makes the last vowel long: `hän puhuu`. Other persons just add the ending.

cards.title: Watch out
cards.body: Vowel harmony works in verbs too: front-vowel verbs take `-vät`: `he kysyvät`, but `he puhuvat`. The ending follows the vowels of the verb.

terms.say: A group of verbs that change in the same way. Finnish has five main groups. You can tell the group from the end of the dictionary form.
The basic form of a verb, the one you find in a dictionary: puhua, syödä, tulla.
The part of a word that stays before the ending. puhu- is the stem of puhua: puhu|n, puhu|t.

lessons.title: Type 1 with stem changes
lessons.objective: Use type 1 verbs whose stem changes, like lukea → luen and ottaa → otan.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Many type 1 verbs have **consonant gradation** in the stem, like the nouns in World 2. The stem is **weak** with `minä, sinä, me, te`. It stays **strong** with `hän` and `he`: `minä luen`, but `hän lukee`.

cards.title: Easy rule
cards.body: Rule of thumb: the endings **-n, -t, -mme, -tte** make the consonant weak. The `hän` and `he` forms keep the strong consonant of the infinitive.

cards.title: Watch out
cards.body: Don't make `hän` weak: it is `hän ottaa`, not *hän otaa*, and `he lukevat`, not *he luevat*.

items.en: I read a newspaper in the café.
Do you know where the shop is?

terms.say: Some consonants in the middle of a word change when an ending is added: kk → k, t → d. In verbs: lukea → luen.

lessons.title: Type 2: syödä, juoda, tehdä
lessons.objective: Use type 2 verbs in the present, including tehdä and nähdä.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Type 2 verbs end in `-da` or `-dä`. Remove it and you have the stem: `syö|dä` → `syö|n`. The `hän` form adds **nothing**: `hän syö`, `hän juo`. The stem already ends in a long vowel or two vowels.

cards.title: Two special verbs
cards.body: `tehdä` (do, make) and `nähdä` (see) are special. Their stem is `tee-` / `näe-`, but `teke-` / `näke-` with `hän` and `he`: `teen`, but `hän tekee`, `he tekevät`.

cards.title: Good to know
cards.body: More useful type 2 verbs: `saada` (get), `voida` (can), `myydä` (sell), `tuoda` (bring). `voida` + infinitive = can do: `Voin tulla.` (I can come.)

items.en: I drink coffee in the morning.
They go to the shop on Saturday.

lessons.title: Type 3: tulla, mennä, opiskella
lessons.objective: Use type 3 verbs (-la, -na, -ra, -sta) in all persons.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Type 3 verbs end in `-la/-lä`, `-na/-nä`, `-ra/-rä` or `-sta/-stä`. Remove the last two letters and add **-e-**: `tul|la` → `tule-` → `tulen`. For `-sta`, remove `-ta`: `pes|tä` → `pese-` → `pesen`.

cards.title: One pattern
cards.body: All four endings: `tulla → tule-`, `mennä → mene-`, `purra` (bite) `→ pure-`, `nousta` (get on) `→ nouse-`. Long verbs too: `opiskella → opiskele-`: `opiskelen`, `hän opiskelee`.

cards.title: Watch out
cards.body: Some type 3 verbs change the consonant the other way, from weak to strong: `kuunnella` (listen) → `kuuntelen` (nn → nt). Learn these with their minä form.

cards.title: olla is irregular
cards.body: `olla` looks like type 3, but it is irregular: `olen, olet, on, olemme, olette, ovat`. You know it from World 1.

items.en: I'll come to the shop at five.
We are going to the café.
I study Finnish in the evening.
He is listening to the radio.

lessons.title: Type 4: haluta, tavata, osata
lessons.objective: Use type 4 verbs, including the strong stem in tavata → tapaan.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Type 4 verbs end in a vowel + `-ta/-tä`: `halu|ta`, `osa|ta`. Remove `-ta` and add **-a/-ä**: `halu` + `a` → `halua-` → `haluan`. The `hän` form ends in a long vowel: `hän haluaa`, `hän osaa`.

cards.title: Gradation the other way
cards.body: In type 4 the **infinitive is weak** and the present stem is **strong**: `tavata` → `tapaan` (v → p), `tykätä` (like) → `tykkään` (k → kk). The strong stem is in every person, also in the negative: `en tapaa`.

cards.title: Watch out
cards.body: Don't add `-n` straight to `halu-` or `osa-`: *halun* and *osan* are wrong. The stem has the extra vowel: `halua|n`, `osaa|n`. Never three vowels in a row: `hän osaa`, not *osaaa*.

cards.title: Use them like this
cards.body: `osata` is for skills: `Osaan vähän suomea.` `haluta` + infinitive: `Haluan ostaa leipää.` `tykätä` takes -sta/-stä: `Tykkään kahvista.`

items.en: We'll meet at the café at three.

lessons.title: Type 5 and the negative
lessons.objective: Use type 5 verbs and make the negative of every verb type.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Type 5 verbs end in `-ita/-itä`. Remove `-ta` and add **-tse-**: `tarvi|ta` → `tarvitse-` → `tarvitsen`. The `hän` form makes the last vowel long: `hän tarvitsee`.

cards.title: The negative of every type
cards.body: The negative is `en, et, ei, emme, ette, eivät` + the **stem without an ending**. Take the minä form and drop `-n`: `luen` → `en lue`, `tapaan` → `en tapaa`, `tarvitsen` → `en tarvitse`.

cards.title: Watch out
cards.body: Only the negative verb changes with the person: `he eivät tule`, never *he eivät tulevat*. And `hän ei lue` (weak, like minä), not *hän ei lukee*.

lessons.title: Genitive: whose?
lessons.objective: Use the genitive singular (-n) for owners and with vieressä, lähellä.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: The **genitive** shows whose something is, like English *'s*: `Anna|n kahvi` = Anna's coffee. The ending is **-n**. The question word is `kenen?` (whose?).

cards.title: Shortcut
cards.body: If you know the -ssa form from World 2, you know the genitive: swap `-ssa` for `-n`. `kaupa|ssa` → `kaupa|n`, `kadu|lla` → `kadu|n`. Both use the weak stem.

cards.title: Next to, near
cards.body: Place words like `vieressä` (next to) and `lähellä` (near) follow a noun in the genitive: `kaupan vieressä` (next to the shop), `pankin lähellä` (near the bank).

cards.title: Watch out
cards.body: In written Finnish, `minun` + noun also needs a suffix (`minun kirjani`), which comes later. For now say `Kirja on minun.` (The book is mine.) or use a name: `Annan kirja`.

items.en: The café is next to the bank.

terms.say: The case that shows who owns something, like 's in English. Ending -n: Annan = Anna's.

lessons.title: Minulla on: I have
lessons.objective: Say what you have and don't have with minulla on / minulla ei ole.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Finnish has no verb *to have*. You say **at me is**: `minulla on` = I have. The owner takes the **adessive** `-lla/-llä` (World 2), and the verb is always `on`.

cards.title: Watch out
cards.body: The verb never changes: `meillä on`, not *meillä olemme*. The negative is always `ei ole`: `minulla ei ole`, not *minulla en ole*.

cards.title: Not only pronouns
cards.body: Names and nouns work the same way: `Annalla on auto.` `Mikolla on koira.` (Mikko → Mikolla, kk → k.)

cards.title: Questions and the negative
cards.body: Ask with `onko`: `Onko sinulla aikaa?` (Do you have time?) In a shop: `Onko teillä maitoa?` In the negative, the thing is in the partitive (next lessons): `Minulla on auto.` → `Minulla ei ole autoa.`

terms.say: The 'on / at' case, ending -lla/-llä. It also shows who has something: minulla on = I have.

lessons.title: Partitive: forms and numbers
lessons.objective: Make the singular partitive and use it after numbers and in prices.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: The **partitive** is a very common case. Its ending is `-a/-ä`, `-ta/-tä` or `-tta/-ttä`. One use: after numbers from 2 up. `yksi kahvi`, but `kaksi kahvia`, `kolme euroa`.

cards.title: Which ending?
head: word ends in
ending
examples
rows: a long vowel or two vowels

cards.title: Watch out
cards.body: **No gradation** in the singular partitive. It keeps the strong form: `kauppa → kauppaa`, `leipä → leipää` (not *leivää*), `lippu → lippua`.

cards.title: -a or -ä?
cards.body: Vowel harmony picks the ending: a, o or u in the word → `-a`: `maito|a`, `sokeri|a`. Only ä, ö, y, e, i → `-ä`: `leipä|ä`, `riisi|ä`, `tee|tä`.

cards.title: Prices
cards.body: Prices use numbers too: `kaksi euroa` (€2), `viisi euroa kaksikymmentä senttiä` (€5.20). After 1 there is no partitive: `yksi euro`. Ask: `Paljonko se maksaa?` (How much does it cost?)

terms.say: A very common case for 'some', amounts and numbers 2+. Endings -a/-ä, -ta/-tä, -tta/-ttä: kahvia, teetä, huonetta.

lessons.title: Partitive: food, amounts, ei ole
lessons.objective: Use the partitive for food and drink, after amount words and after ei ole.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Use the partitive for **an amount of something you don't count**: food and drinks like `kahvia`, `maitoa`, `juustoa`. English often says *some* or nothing: `Juon teetä.` = I drink tea.

cards.title: Amount words
cards.body: After amount words the noun is partitive: `vähän maitoa` (a little milk), `paljon kahvia` (a lot of coffee), `kilo juustoa`, `litra maitoa`, `kuppi teetä`, `pala kakkua`.

cards.title: ei ole + partitive
cards.body: In a negative 'there is' or 'I have' sentence, the thing is partitive: `Kaupassa on maitoa.` → `Kaupassa ei ole maitoa.` `Minulla on auto.` → `Minulla ei ole autoa.`

cards.title: Two special words
cards.body: Two everyday words are irregular: `vesi` → `vettä` (lasi vettä = a glass of water) and `lapsi` → `lasta` (kaksi lasta = two children). Learn them as chunks.

items.en: There's a little milk in the fridge.
I drink a lot of coffee.
There's no bread in the shop.

lessons.title: Verbs that take the partitive
lessons.objective: Use the partitive after haluta, tarvita, rakastaa and odottaa.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Some verbs always want the partitive. Learn them in pairs: `rakastaa` + partitive (love), `odottaa` + partitive (wait for). `Odotan bussia.` `Rakastan sinua.`

cards.title: haluta and tarvita
cards.body: With food, drinks and other amounts, `haluta` and `tarvita` take the partitive: `Haluan teetä.` `Tarvitsen apua.` In the negative **every** object is partitive: `En halua kahvia.`

cards.title: Watch out
cards.body: English says *wait for*. Finnish has no extra word: `Odotan sinua.` (I'm waiting for you.) Not *odotan sinulle*.

cards.title: Memory hook
cards.body: Love and waiting never really end, so they take the 'unfinished' case: the partitive.

items.en: I'm waiting for you at the café.
Would you like coffee or tea?

lessons.title: At the café and the shop
lessons.objective: Order at a café, ask prices and write a short invitation or shopping message.

cards.title: At the café
cards.body: Useful chunks: `Mitä saa olla?` (What would you like?), `Yksi kahvi ja pulla, kiitos.`, `Täällä vai mukaan?` (For here or to go?), `Tuleeko muuta?` (Anything else?).

items.fi: Kaksi teetä ja yksi pulla, kiitos.
items.en: Two teas and one bun, please.

cards.title: A shopping message
cards.body: A shopping list uses the basic form: `maito, leipä, juusto`. In a message, use whole sentences: `Meillä ei ole kahvia.` `Tarvitsemme maitoa.` `Voitko ostaa leipää?`

cards.title: An invitation
cards.body: Say what, when and where, then ask: `Haluatko tulla?` or `Voitko tulla?` End with a friendly line: `Odotan vastausta!` (I'm waiting for your answer!) and your name.

cards.title: Prices
cards.body: Finnish writes prices with a comma: `2,50 €`. Say `kaksi euroa viisikymmentä senttiä`. At the checkout you may hear: `Kortilla vai käteisellä?` (By card or in cash?)

cards.title: Put it together
cards.body: Mix what you know: verb types (`ostan, juon, tulen, haluan, tarvitsen`), `minulla on`, and the partitive after numbers and amounts.

questions.explain: Type 1: remove -a from asua to get the stem asu-, then add the me ending -mme: asumme.
Type 1, he form: stem puhu- + -vat. puhua has back vowels (u, a), so the ending is -vat, not -vät.

wrong: Type 1 ends in two vowels, like puhua.
questions.explain: Infinitives ending in -ita/-itä are type 5: tarvita, valita.

wrong: ostaa ends in two vowels: type 1.
questions.explain: Type 2 verbs end in -da or -dä: juoda, syödä, tehdä.
Subject + verb + object: He puhuvat suomea. A language after puhua is in the partitive (suomea).

questions.audio: Hei! Minä olen Leo. Asun Turussa. Puhun englantia ja vähän suomea.
questions.explain: “Asun Turussa” = I live in Turku. asua (type 1): minä asun.
lukea has k → ∅ gradation. The minä ending -n makes the stem weak: luke- → lue- → luen.
The hän form keeps the strong stem (no gradation): luke- + long vowel = lukee.
ottaa has tt → t. The me ending -mme makes it weak: otta- → ota- → otamme.
questions.source: Uusi kielemme: Consonant gradation in verbs

questions.explain: ymmärtää has rt → rr gradation. With the minä ending -n the stem is weak: ymmärrä- → ymmärrän.

wrong: hän keeps the strong tt: ottaa.
minä takes the weak t: otan.
he keeps the strong tt: ottavat.
questions.explain: Gradation in type 1: weak with minä, sinä, me, te; strong with hän and he. So hän ottaa, minä otan.
questions.source: Uusi kielemme: Consonant gradation in verbs

questions.q: Build the sentence: “I understand a little Finnish.”
questions.explain: vähän (a little) comes before the word it describes: vähän suomea. ymmärrän = minä form of ymmärtää (rt → rr).

questions.audio: Aamulla luen lehteä. Liisa lukee kirjaa. Me juomme kahvia keittiössä.
wrong: The speaker reads the newspaper (luen lehteä).
questions.explain: “Liisa lukee kirjaa” = Liisa reads a book. lukee is the hän form of lukea (strong k).
Type 2: remove -da from juoda to get the stem juo-, then add -n: juon.
Type 2 hän form: just the stem, nothing added, because syö- already ends in two vowels: hän syö.
tehdä is special: the stem is tee- (teen), but hän and he use teke-: hän tekee, he tekevät.

questions.q: Which is the hän form of `nähdä` (to see)?
wrong: näe is the negative stem: hän ei näe.
This is not a form: hän uses the stem näke-.
questions.explain: nähdä works like tehdä: minä näen, but hän näkee and he näkevät.
With me the ending is -mme: juo- + -mme = juomme.

questions.q: Build the sentence: “Can you come tomorrow?”
questions.explain: voida + infinitive: voit + -ko question = Voitko, then the infinitive tulla. huomenna (tomorrow) can go at the end.

questions.audio: Aamulla syön puuroa ja juon teetä. Lapset syövät leipää ja juovat maitoa.
questions.explain: “Lapset … juovat maitoa” = the children drink milk. juovat is the he form of juoda.
Type 3: remove -la and add -e-: tule-, then the minä ending -n: tulen.
Type 3: mennä → stem mene-, then -mme: menemme.
opiskella → stem opiskele-. The hän form makes the last vowel long: opiskelee.
kuunnella has gradation the other way: weak nn in the infinitive, strong nt in the present stem: kuuntele- → kuuntelen.

questions.q: Which is the minä form of `pestä` (to wash)?
wrong: Don't add -n to the infinitive. The stem is pese-.
The long vowel belongs to hän: hän pesee.
questions.explain: -sta/-stä verbs: remove -ta/-tä and add -e-: pes|tä → pese- → pesen.

questions.q: Which is the hän form of `opiskella`?
wrong: opiskele is the negative stem: hän ei opiskele.
The ll of the infinitive is not in the stem: opiskele-.
questions.explain: Type 3: opiskel|la → opiskele-. hän makes the last vowel long: opiskelee.

questions.q: Build the sentence: “They are going to the café.”
questions.explain: mennä → he menevät (front vowels, so -vät). To where? → illative: kahvilaan.

questions.audio: Hei! Olen Maria. Opiskelen suomea. Tänään menen kirjastoon ja sitten kauppaan.
questions.q: Where is Maria going first today?
wrong: She goes to the shop after that (sitten = then).
questions.explain: “Menen kirjastoon ja sitten kauppaan” = I'm going to the library and then to the shop.
Type 4: halu|ta → halu + a = halua-, then -n: haluan.
osata → stem osaa-. The hän form is just the stem, because it already ends in a long vowel: hän osaa.
tavata has v → p, with the strong p in the present stem: tapaa- + -mme = tapaamme.
tykätä: the infinitive has weak k, the present stem has strong kk: tykkää- → tykkään. It takes -sta: kahvista.

questions.q: Which is the minä form of `tavata` (to meet)?
wrong: Type 4 uses the strong stem: v → p.
The stem needs the extra vowel: tapaa-n. (tapan is from tappaa, 'to kill'!)
questions.explain: Type 4 present stem: strong consonant + extra vowel: tavata → tapaa- → tapaan.

questions.q: Which form fits? Sinä ___ suomea hyvin.
wrong: The stem has two a's: osaa-t.
questions.explain: osata → osaa-, sinä ending -t: osaat.

questions.q: Build the sentence: “Do you want tea?”
questions.explain: The verb with -ko comes first in a yes/no question: Haluatko sinä teetä? Tea is an amount, so partitive: teetä.

questions.audio: Minä ja Jussi tapaamme huomenna kahvilassa kello kaksi. Haluatko tulla mukaan?
questions.explain: “Tapaamme huomenna … kello kaksi” = we meet tomorrow at two. tapaamme is the me form of tavata.
Type 5: tarvi|ta → tarvitse-, then -n: tarvitsen.
Type 5: vali|ta → valitse-, sinä ending -t: valitset.
Negative: en + the stem without a personal ending. juon → en juo.
Negative: ei + stem. The stem is the same for every person: tulen → (ei) tule.
Only eivät shows the person. The main verb is the stem: haluan → (eivät) halua.

wrong: The main verb has no personal ending in the negative.
With he the negative verb is eivät.
Not the infinitive: use the stem tule.
questions.explain: Negative = eivät (the person) + the verb stem: He eivät tule.

questions.q: What is the negative of `minä luen`?
wrong: Drop the -n: the main verb has no ending.
lukee is the hän form; the negative uses the weak stem lue.
Use the weak stem, as in luen: k → ∅.
questions.explain: Take the minä form and drop -n: luen → en lue. The stem is weak, like in minä luen.

questions.q: Build the sentence: “I don't need a bag.”
questions.explain: en + stem tarvitse. In a negative sentence the object is partitive: kassia.

questions.audio: Tarvitsetko kassin? – Ei kiitos, en tarvitse. Minulla on oma kassi.
questions.q: Does the customer need a bag?
wrong: They say: Ei kiitos, en tarvitse (No thanks, I don't need).
questions.explain: “En tarvitse. Minulla on oma kassi.” = I don't need one. I have my own bag.
Genitive = owner + -n: Anna → Annan (Anna's).
vieressä follows the genitive. pankki has kk → k: pankissa → pankin.
lähellä follows the genitive. kauppa has pp → p in the weak stem: kaupan.

questions.hint: in the centre of the city
questions.explain: keskusta of the city → genitive. kaupunki has nk → ng: kaupungissa → kaupungin.

questions.q: Kenen auto tämä on? What does `kenen` ask?
questions.explain: kenen is the genitive of kuka: whose? Kenen auto? = Whose car?

wrong: t → d in the weak stem, as in kadulla.
katua is the partitive, which keeps the strong t.
kadulla is the adessive, 'on the street'.
questions.explain: katu has t → d gradation: the genitive uses the weak stem: kadu|n.

questions.q: Build the sentence: “The café is next to the shop.”
questions.explain: The noun in the genitive comes before vieressä: kaupan vieressä.

questions.audio: Uusi kahvila on nyt auki! Kahvila on pankin vieressä, Kauppakadulla. Tervetuloa!
wrong: kaupan = the shop's; the text says pankin (the bank's).
It is next to the bank (vieressä), not inside it.
questions.explain: “Pankin vieressä” = next to the bank. pankin is the genitive of pankki.
Possession: owner in the adessive + on. sinä → sinulla.

questions.q: Mikko asuu Espoossa, ja ___ on iso talo. (hän)
questions.explain: hän in the adessive is hänellä: hänellä on = he has.
In possession sentences the verb is always ei ole in the negative, for every person: meillä ei ole.

questions.q: Which form fits? Minulla ___ kaksi lasta.
wrong: olen = I am; possession uses minulla on.
questions.explain: With minulla, sinulla, hänellä… the verb is always on: Minulla on kaksi lasta.

questions.q: Which sentence means *We don't have a car*?
wrong: After ei ole the thing is partitive: autoa.
This means 'we are not a car'.
The verb is always ei ole: meillä ei ole.
questions.explain: Owner in -lla + ei ole + the thing in the partitive: Meillä ei ole autoa.

questions.q: Build the sentence: “Do you have time today?”
questions.explain: onko + owner (sinulla) + the thing. Time is an amount, so partitive: aikaa.

questions.audio: Hei! Minulla on huomenna vapaapäivä. Onko sinulla aikaa? Haluatko tulla kahville?
questions.q: Why does the speaker have time tomorrow?
wrong: Only one free day: vapaapäivä = day off.
questions.explain: “Minulla on huomenna vapaapäivä” = I have a day off tomorrow.
After numbers 2+ the noun is partitive. kahvi ends in one short vowel and has a back vowel: kahvi + a.
Prices: number 2+ + partitive. euro + a = euroa.
After neljä the noun is partitive. banaani has back vowels, so -a: banaania.
Words ending in -e take -tta/-ttä in the partitive: huone → huonetta.

wrong: No gradation in the singular partitive: pp stays.
lippu has u, a back vowel, so -a.
questions.explain: Number 2+ → partitive. The singular partitive keeps the strong form: lippu → lippua.

wrong: The partitive singular keeps the strong p.
-tä is for words ending in a long vowel, like teetä.
questions.explain: leipä ends in one short vowel → add -ä (front vowels), no gradation: leipää.

questions.q: Build the sentence: “The bread costs three euros.”
questions.explain: maksaa = costs. After the number kolme comes the partitive euroa.

questions.audio: Mitä saa olla? – Kaksi kahvia ja yksi pulla, kiitos. – Se tekee kuusi euroa.
wrong: kaksi (two) is the number of coffees.
questions.explain: “Se tekee kuusi euroa” = That comes to six euros. kuusi + partitive euroa.

questions.audio: Kahvi maksaa kaksi euroa viisikymmentä senttiä. Tee maksaa kaksi euroa. Pulla maksaa kolme euroa.
wrong: That is the price of coffee.
That is the price of the bun.
questions.explain: “Tee maksaa kaksi euroa” = Tea costs two euros.
After amount words like vähän the noun is partitive: maito + a = maitoa.
paljon + partitive. vesi is irregular: its partitive is vettä.
ei ole + partitive. leipä keeps the strong p in the partitive: leipää.
Negative possession: minulla ei ole + partitive. raha + a = rahaa.

questions.q: Read the note: *Hei! Jääkaapissa on maitoa ja juustoa, mutta meillä ei ole leipää eikä kahvia.* What do they need to buy?
wrong: They have milk and cheese (jääkaapissa on…).
questions.explain: “Meillä ei ole leipää eikä kahvia” = we have no bread and no coffee. ei ole + partitive.

questions.q: Which sentence means *There is no milk in the shop*?
wrong: After ei ole the thing is partitive: maitoa.
questions.explain: Place in -ssa + ei ole + partitive: Kaupassa ei ole maitoa.

questions.q: Build the sentence: “There is a little milk in the fridge.”
questions.explain: Place + on + amount: Jääkaapissa on vähän maitoa. After vähän the noun is partitive.

questions.audio: Anteeksi, onko teillä ruisleipää? – Ei valitettavasti. Tänään meillä ei ole ruisleipää, mutta huomenna on.
wrong: Tänään meillä ei ole = today we don't have any.
They say it will be there tomorrow.
questions.explain: “…mutta huomenna on” = but tomorrow there is (some). ei ole + partitive: ruisleipää.
odottaa always takes the partitive: bussi + a = bussia.
rakastaa always takes the partitive. sinä → sinua.
Type 1: rakasta- + -vat = rakastavat. The object is partitive: suklaata (suklaa ends in a long vowel → -ta).
In the negative the object is always partitive. tee ends in a long vowel → -tä: teetä.

wrong: No 'for' word in Finnish: odottaa takes the partitive.
questions.explain: odottaa + partitive: Odotan sinua asemalla = I'm waiting for you at the station.

questions.q: Build the sentence: “Would you like coffee or tea?”
questions.explain: Question with -ko + both drinks in the partitive. vai = or (in questions).

questions.q: Build the sentence: “They are waiting for the bus at the station.”
questions.explain: odottaa + partitive: bussia. At the station = adessive: asemalla.

questions.audio: Hei Sami! Odotan sinua kahvilassa ikkunan vieressä. Tarvitsetko jotain? Täällä on hyvää kakkua.
options: At the station by the door
In the shop by the checkout
In the café by the window
wrong: The speaker is in the café (kahvilassa).
The speaker is in the café, not at home.
questions.explain: “Odotan sinua kahvilassa ikkunan vieressä” = I'm waiting for you in the café by the window.
'By card' uses the adessive -lla (World 2). kortti has tt → t in the weak stem: kortilla.
Type 2, he form: syö- + -vät (front vowels). The object is partitive: jäätelöä.
After kaksi the noun is partitive, with no gradation: lippu → lippua.
lähellä follows the genitive: asema + n = aseman.

questions.q: At a café you hear *Täällä vai mukaan?* What do they want to know?
options: Whether you eat here or take it away
wrong: That would be Kortilla vai käteisellä?
That would be Mitä saa olla?
questions.explain: täällä = here, mukaan = with you (to go). The server asks if you stay or take it away.

questions.q: Read the sign: *Tarjous! Kahvi ja pulla 4,50 €. Joka päivä kello 8–11.* What is true?
options: The offer is only at weekends
The offer is in the evening
wrong: 4,50 € is for coffee and a bun together.
questions.explain: Joka päivä kello 8–11 = every day from 8 to 11. tarjous = special offer.

questions.q: Build the sentence: “We don't have any coffee.”
questions.explain: Owner (meillä) + ei ole + partitive: kahvia.

questions.q: Build the sentence: “We'll meet at the café at three.”
questions.explain: tavata → tapaamme (strong p). In the café = kahvilassa; at three = kello kolme.

questions.audio: Mitä saa olla? – Yksi tee ja kaksi pullaa, kiitos. – Tuleeko muuta? – Ei kiitos. Maksan kortilla.
wrong: käteisellä = in cash; the customer says kortilla.
questions.explain: “Maksan kortilla” = I'll pay by card.

questions.audio: Tervetuloa! Tänään juusto on tarjouksessa. Kilo juustoa maksaa kahdeksan euroa.
wrong: kaksi is two; the price is kahdeksan (eight).
questions.explain: “Kilo juustoa maksaa kahdeksan euroa” = a kilo of cheese costs eight euros.

writing.title: Invite a friend
writing.situation: You are having a small birthday party at home on Saturday. Write a message to your Finnish friend Sanna and invite her.
points: what food and drinks you will have
one thing your friend can bring
writing.model: Hei Sanna! Mitä kuuluu? Minulla on lauantaina syntymäpäivä. Haluatko tulla meille? Juhla alkaa kello kuusi. Asun Rantakadulla 4. Teen pizzaa ja kakkua, ja meillä on kahvia ja teetä. Voitko tuoda vähän mehua? Odotan vastausta! Terveisin, Tom
checklist: I gave the day, time and address
Food and drinks are in the partitive (pizzaa, kahvia)

writing.title: A shopping message
writing.situation: You are at work. Your partner Anna is going to the shop after work. Send her a message about what you need at home.
points: what you don't have at home
what you need and how much
writing.model: Hei Anna! Menetkö kauppaan tänään? Meillä ei ole maitoa eikä leipää. Tarvitsemme myös kuusi kananmunaa ja vähän juustoa. Voitko ostaa kahvia? Kahvi on tarjouksessa. Kiitos! Nähdään illalla. Mikko
checklist: Food after tarvita and amount words is partitive
I said thanks and signed my name

writing.title: At the café
writing.situation: You are waiting for your friend Sami at a café. He is late. Send him a message.
points: what you are eating or drinking
writing.model: Hei Sami! Olen jo kahvilassa. Juon teetä ja syön pullaa. Haluatko kahvia vai teetä? Täällä on myös hyvää kakkua. Pala maksaa neljä euroa. Odotan sinua ikkunan vieressä. Nähdään pian! Lisa
checklist: Food and drinks are in the partitive
I said where I sit (… vieressä)
